newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining: Kazakh El Dorado?
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION - Louthean on Australian Mining: Kazakh El Dorado?

text.p: By Ross Louthean*
The windswept steppes of a part of old Russia is now the focal point for exploration for gold, base metals and oil.

The independent Kazakhstan is now luring a mix of miners wanting to add a new frontier with all its raw potential, and juniors emanating from Canada, Australia and Europe with the hope that their new tenements will be company makers.
But it hasn't been all beer and skittles with the emergence of Kazakhstan from the yoke of communism and its inherent commercial inefficiencies.
Kazakhstan has, like many other former Russian dependencies like Mongolia, moved on a tenuous course towards economic health with the old umbilical cord cut and debt staring it in the face.

The predicament was not helped by a 48 percent slump in its mining and metals sector between 1990-94 though international stockbroking firm ABN-Amro believes Kazakhstan is now through the worst of its transition from communism and is ready to stage an economic recovery.

Kazakhstan used to provide 30 percent of the copper, 64 percent of the lead, 46 percent of the zinc and 99 percent of chromite for the original Soviet economy. Gold mining was given a fillip when President Nursultan Nazarbayev signed a new Gold Law which allowed for the export of gold.
BIG DEPOSITS BUT POLITICAL RISK REMAINS EVIDENT

Some other observers see warts in the blue sky mining scenario. The international division of Australia's J.B. Were & Son, based in New York, considers modern gold mining pioneer Bakyrchik Gold Plc should retain a discount tag because political risk in Kazakhstan is still evident.

London-listed Bakyrchik owns 40 percent of the Bakyrchik mine with the Kazak Government holding the balance. Recently the drawn-out expansion programme set by Bakyrchik Gold saw the need to raise extra capital to continue, and the white knight was North American entrepreneur Robert Friedland of Diamond Fields Resources fame who gained a major re-funding.

But the objective is high, for the mining-milling expansion blueprint for the Bakyrchik mine is to lift production initially to 250,000 ounces, then to 750,000 oz based on tapping a gold system with sulphide ore resources of 34.2 million tonnes grading 7.37 grams/tonne gold and oxide resources of 4.3 mt a 2.6 g/t.
The known deposit is on a structure 17 km long, and Kazakhstan has a lot of geological allures of this size.
Friedland not only has put fiscal props under Bakyrchik Gold but has his Indochina Goldfields Ltd now in the Kazakhstan scene.

Other companies holding ground or undertaking exploration-development deals are Amax Gold Inc, Goldbelt Resources Ltd, William Resources Ltd, Placer Dome Inc, Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp (now linked to Homestake Mining) and Perth-administered and Vancouver-backed Steppe Gold Resources Ltd run by a group associated with John Menzies.
Menzies, who operates a group of companies and is a prime backer of proposed Perth gold float Aarex Goldfields NL which has a huge package of lands in the traditional goldfields of Western Australia.

He is a keen advocate of Kazakhstan and will this year move his home base from Perth to Vancouver, close to the money markets and a Canadian scene that has shown a great zeal for Indonesia, West Africa and now Kazakhstan.

In the mid 1996 a new mining law was introduced which some observers believe addresses many of the concerns of Western investors, and this Law on Subsoil provides mineral rights to be owned by the State, not unlike the Crown holding the rights in Australian States.
KAZAKHSTAN'S TAX SYSTEM DRASTICALLY REFORMED

In a resume of the political and financial scene, Steppe Gold said that Kazakhstan's taxation system has been drastically reformed by a mid 1995 initiative signed by President Nazarbayev. This included deduction of production and development costs, and depreciation on the cost of capital equipment, as well as carrying forward of losses and the offsetting of taxes payable outside of Kazakhstan.

Menzies said a recent amendment saw exemption of exploration and prospecting activity from payment of value added taxes. A foreign entity is subject to a withholding tax on repatriated profits at 15 percent, while dividends payable by legal entities are subject to withholding tax, also at 15 percent.

At a 1995 London seminar Prime Minister Kazhegeldin said Kazakhstan was looking at a policy of employment and the reform of education and industry where countries of the former Soviet Union were behind the times. He felt that in principal the progress should see the government cutting free of a dependence on foreign borrowings after 1998.
This was an evolutionary stage and he said people were now coming to government better trained and understanding policymaking and the need to make a profit.

At that same conference Britain's Minister of Industry and Energy, Tim Eggar, said that after four years of independence Kazakhstan bore little resemblance to the former Soviet satellite. Nevertheless it was a country where quick profits would be difficult and he urged any newcomers to consult the foreign companies already established there.

Late last year ING Barings pointed to tighter government policy curbing inflation which was 60 percent in 1995 but progressively brought down to a rate of 2.1 percent in August. When the tenge currency replaced the rouble at the end of 1993 the exchange rate with the Greenback dollar was Tenge 5.0 to US$1 but by the end of 1995 it had reached T55.4/US$1 and had fallen further to T75.60 last Friday.
KAZAKHSTAN "THE CHILE OF THE NEXT DECADE"?

The chairman of Kazakhstan Minerals Corp (KazMinCo), Anthony Williams, said Kazakhstan is not utopia. "I can tell you that; but the prize is worth the trouble. It will be the Chile of the next decade."

London-based and also Toronto listed KazMinCo is certainly drilling big structures. The 50 percent owned Samarskoye porphyry copper-gold project has produced wide intersections, including 514 metres starting at 266m depth grading 1.01 percent copper and 0.31 grams/tonne gold. One other hole produced 103m at 4.98 percent copper and 1.32 g/t gold followed by 324m at 3.04 percent copper and 0.88 g/t gold. Samarskoye is just north of Karaganda in central Kazakhstan.
On another prime property, Varvarinskoye (49 percent) near the Russian border, drill hits have included 29.1m at 6.1 g/t gold and 4.94 percent copper and 46.3m at 4.15 g/t gold and 3.34 copper.
Drilling results in early 1996 saw KazMinCo's shares soar in North American dealing. The results, from Samarskoye, included an intercept of 195m at 2.2 percent copper and 0.63 percent copper.

In a study of KazMinCo, Yorkton Securities estimated prior to the successful 1996 drilling that Varvarinskoye had a resource of 61 million tonnes at 6.4 percent g/t gold and 1.4 percent copper, Sarmarskoye had 130 mt at 1.17 percent copper and 0.5 g/t gold and among other projects, Svetinskoye 1.5mt at 10.5 g/t gold, Satyrgul 34 mt at 3.5 percent copper and 0.7 g/t gold and nearby Zhaisan 11 mt at 3.3 percent copper and 0.8 g/t gold.
* Ross Louthean is editor of Paydirt and publisher of Gold Mining Journal, The Australian Mines Handbook and Mineral Resources of New Zealand.
